This paper introduces Codec Avatar Studio, a novel dataset designed to facilitate the creation of photorealistic, driveable, and generalizable avatars. The dataset includes paired captures of 256 subjects' heads in two modalities: high-resolution multi-view scans and internal camera video from a VR headset—along with full-body multi-modal captures of four subjects. These datasets aim to address the challenges of generalization and driveability in avatar creation by providing both high-quality and low-resource capture setups. The paper also releases pre-trained models to support the community in advancing avatar generation research.
After the rebuttal, the paper received all positive recommendations (two "marginally above acceptance" ratings and two "good paper, accept" ratings). The primary concerns from reviewers included questions about the scale and generalizability claims, as well as the ethics and consent procedures for the dataset. The authors addressed these issues by clarifying the distinction between generalization and completeness, elaborating on the consent process, and providing additional experimental results. The AC agrees with the reviewers' assessments and recommends accepting the paper.

I want to thank the authors for the rebuttal.

I am inclined to keep my rating. I expect the authors to include at least some of the details provided in the rebuttal in the main paper (e.g. info detailing where the ground truth comes from, and experimental results). I would also encourage authors to elaborate on the motivation for the choice of the headset capture for the head, and phone for the body which was one of my questions in the review, however, left unanswered. The other thing to add would be clarification regarding A4 (e.g. the estimated release size of RenderMe, or size per identity vs the same for yours - should show the benefit of curating the compression process).

We thank all the reviewers for their comments. All reviewers have commented on the value of having high quality data for avatar modelling, which is not often available to academic labs. Reviewers also appreciate the value of our pre-trained models and baselines, as well as the effort put towards making the data size manageable.

We now address shared concerns among the reviewers.

> **Q1.** More details about consent

**A1:** Several reviewers asked for more details about the consent forms used in the study. The forms contain our contact information, the purpose of the study, a description of the capture devices and capture procedures, and the estimated time the study will take. Additionally, the forms state that participation is voluntary, that participants may withdraw at any time and still get compensated for their time, that the data will be used for research purposes, and that Meta is the licenser and owner of the collected data, which may be distributed to third parties in the future. Note that participants keep a copy of the consent form after the study.

> **Q2.** Experimental results

**A2:** We are adding experimental results and official protocols for all the models that we ship.

For Goliath, we go over the validation set of each capture, and evaluate PSNR in the masked region given by our segmentation:

|  | AXE977 | QVC422 | QZX685 | XKT970 |

| Clothed body | 37.20 | 39.72 | 43.24 | 39.95 |
| Minimally clothed body | 41.50 | 41.04 | 46.13 | 40.06 |

For Ava-256, we hold 16 subjects for validation and train on the other 240. We evaluate $\ell_1$ error:

| --- | ---: |

| NCC597 | 8.70 |

| NNQ107 | 10.54 |

| PGO261 | 14.70 |

| UIQ957 | 7.42 |
| UMQ592 | 7.84 |
| YIK625 | 9.17 |
| ZEL435 | 8.20 |
| ZUS575 | 8.78 |

> **Q3.** Qualitative results

**A3:** Please refer to the attached PDF for qualitative results of the models that we provide with Goliath-4. For qualitative samples on validation subjects on Ava-256, please see https://github.com/facebookresearch/ava-256/blob/main/viz/eval.md.

> **Q4.** Experimenting with other datasets

**A4:** Experimenting with previous datasets is difficult for a couple of reasons. On the one hand, for Ava-256, our multi-person reconstruction algorithms rely on having high quality pre-computed assets such as registration and unwrapped textures; obtaining these assets for other datasets requires a large engineering effort, and is something that we believe should be addressed orthogonally to our work. On the other hand, Goliath-4 provides the first publicly available relightable head and hand captures that we are aware of, so comparison of relightable models on previous datasets is not possible.

> **Q1** The usage and models for this data should be further discussed in the main paper, including comparisons of trained models on previous datasets and the effectiveness of the data on the provided tasks.

**A1:** This is a shared concern among reviewers. Please refer to the common rebuttal above.

**A2:** Please refer to the shared rebuttal for quantitative results of our models, and to the attached PDF for qualitative results.

> **Q3** In the related work, add one more table to compare with existing body avatars and hand avatars.

**A3:** Thank you for your suggestion. We will include a comparison in Table form with current body and hand avatars in the final version of our paper.

> **Q4** The main issue of this work is about the quantity. Although the size is large (32TB), the IDs, sentences and expressions are limited compared with previous head and body avatar datasets, making the in-the-wild generalization poor.

**A4:**  Please note that, for faces specifically, RenderMe is indeed the largest published dataset we are aware of (accepted a year ago to this very same track). However, most of the data in RenderMe has not been made available to the public (see https://renderme-360.github.io/inner-download.html#Download). In particular, only 21 subjects are provided in full, while for the rest of the subjects only a few keyframes are available – with a variable number of cameras, and without assets. FaceScape has 359 multi-view captures, but fewer views (68 vs 80) and expressions (20 vs 35) than our dataset. Finally, HUMBI Face [66] has much lower resolution (200 x 150 for faces), and unfortunately we never obtained access to i3DMM, which has only 64 identities. Therefore, Ava-256 is comparable to the largest multi-view face datasets publicly available to date.

MVHumanNet and DNA rendering are indeed impressive and very recent works that push the boundary of available full-body captures. However, full-body captures, even at high resolution, end up with relatively low-resolution for the face and hands, which are the parts of the human body that people use the most to communicate. Here, we believe that paired face and hand captures are vital to engaging telepresence, which motivates our Goliath release.

We are glad to see that reviewer Hqoy thinks that our dataset is excellent, and would promote the evolution of the field of digital human construction.

> **Q1.** The compression rate of JPEG and other methods used in this work is limited. It is recommended to use more advanced VVC, WEBP, etc.

**A1.** Thanks for the suggestion. We note that, while we benchmarked JPEG, we did not use that format for the dataset release; rather, we used AVIF, which turned out to have the best compression ratio in our experiments.

We have also considered using VVC and other video formats such as AV1 and H256; however, we have decided against video codecs because they greatly increase the complexity for decoding on the user’s end – note that the dataset contains over 200 million images, so this would require substantial computational resources for decompressing the dataset. Moreover, if the dataset is left compressed, random access becomes more computationally expensive. Finally, from datasets such as HumanEva [1] , we know it can be difficult to find the specific video codec and ensure that a particular frame number is extracted; which is much simpler with images.

As suggested, we have added WebP to our compression benchmark. Please refer to the attached PDF to see this new comparison.

> **Q2.** The main contribution of this article lies in the dataset, but what advantages does this dataset have compared to previous ones? For example, is the semantic segmentation provided in Assets more accurate than the previous ones? Or is using this large-scale dataset to train tasks such as avatar singing better than a small-scale one? These all require objective indicators, and the indicators listed in Table 2 alone are not enough to prove the advantages. In other words, articles in the db track need to explain and solve a certain problem or address a problem that no one before has solved it. If the data scale is just dozens of times larger than the previous work, this article can be an excellent technical report, but not a research paper.

**A2:** The main advantage of Ava-256, compared to other datasets, is the availability of paired high-definition dome captures with headset captures for 256 subjects, enabling the study and reproducibility of avatar driving from VR headsets, such as [4, 5]. We emphasize that there are currently no other publicly available datasets with this composition. While we provide a baseline implementation of a model that produces high-fidelity avatars with disentangled identity and expression, building robust methods for avatar driving from sensors with limited views is an open area of research that is outside the scope of our work.

Similarly, the main advantage of Goliath-4 compared to other datasets is the availability of paired relightable head and hand captures, normal and minimally clothed captures, and mobile phone version of all these captures for the same subjects, enabling the study of both complete body reconstruction with high-detailed heads and hands, as well as avatar construction from mobile captures. Studies like UCA [2] and UHM [3] relied on private data to study the relation between phone and dome captures; with Goliath-4, we would like to enable systems like that to work with public data, and extend them to high quality full-body from phone data or the relation between minimal and clothed data, among others.
Again, there are no publicly-available datasets with this composition. In this case, we also provide baselines for full body, hands, and head reconstruction, but full reconstruction using all high-definition captures and building avatars from mobile captures are both outside the scope of our work.

**References:**

- [1] Sigal, L. et al, Humaneva: Synchronized video and motion capture dataset and baseline algorithm for evaluation of articulated human motion, in IJCV 2010
- [2] Cao, Chen, et al, Authentic volumetric avatars from a phone scan, in SIGGRAPH 2022.
- [3] Moon, G. et al, Authentic Hand Avatar from a Phone Scan via Universal Hand Model, in CVPR 2024
- [4] Bai, Shaojie, et al, Universal Facial Encoding of Codec Avatars from VR Headsets, in SIGGRAPH 2024
- [5] Patel, S, et al. Fast Registration of Photorealistic Avatars for VR Facial Animation, in ECCV 2024

We are glad to hear that reviewer uYLj thinks our dataset is of sufficient quality and interest to the research community, and notes that the data is not usually available to academic labs.

> **Q1.** Ethics and consent from subjects

**A1:** Please refer to the common rebuttal for more details on our consent forms.

> **Q2.** I find the claims on the use of the datasets towards generalizable reconstruction and "complete" models to be an overrepresentation of the dataset (note this is in the title of the submission), specially given that the scale on the "complete" data is very limited at only 4 subject identities.

**A2:** Our claims of generalization and completeness are orthogonal: Ava-256 enables the budding research area of avatar generalization to novel faces, while Goliath-4 enables completeness (in terms of body modelling) for a single individual. We will clarify this in the final version of the paper.

> **Q3.** Recent dataset releases, such as MVHumanNet (full body, +5000 subjects), DNA-Rendering, RenderMe have order of magnitudes more identities while also keeping a dense sampling of cameras at high resolution. In essence, this means Ava-256 and Goliath-4 might be outdate quickly in terms of scale.

**A3:** Please note that, for faces specifically, RenderMe is indeed the largest published dataset we are aware of (accepted a year ago to this very same track). However, most of the data in RenderMe has not been made available to the public (see https://renderme-360.github.io/inner-download.html#Download). In particular, only 21 subjects are provided in full, while for the rest of the subjects only a few keyframes are available – with a variable number of cameras, and _without_ assets. FaceScape has 359 multi-view captures, but fewer views (68 vs 80) and expressions (20 vs 35) than our dataset. Finally, HUMBI Face [66] has much lower resolution (200 x 150 for faces), and unfortunately we never obtained access to i3DMM, which has only 64 identities. Therefore, Ava-256 is comparable to the largest multi-view face datasets publicly available to date, and is not orders of magnitude smaller than other releases.

MVHumanNet and DNA rendering are indeed impressive recent works that push the boundary of available full-body captures. However, full-body captures, even at high resolution, end up with relatively low-resolution for the face and hands, which are the parts of the human body that people use the most to communicate. Here, we believe that paired face and hand captures are vital for telepresence, which motivates our Goliath release.

> **Q4.** In general the submission is not providing a lot of technical details and insight about the exact composition of the capturing set-up (e.g. camera and light models, calibration procedures) [...].

**A4:** The face and hand capture dome uses ~170 cameras (Sony IMX253 sensor) with pixel size 3.45 μm, shutter speed of 2.222 ms and 35mm lenses. The body capture dome uses ~230 cameras (with the same sensor) and images are captured with a 1ms exposure.

The relightable setup consists of ~400 white LED lights (SmartVision SX30) and in-house software to control each light’s intensity. Fully lit frames have all lights turned on with short pulses (120us), while Groups of 5 lights have 2.2ms pulses. For heads, every third frame is fully-lit, and for hands every other frame is fully-lit. 

Calibration is done with a robotic arm that holds a patterned icosahedron on its end, following Ha et al [1], and is performed before every capture.

Many challenges arise when building a system of this magnitude; for example, the software to control the robotic arm, the cameras, and to store a capture with ~170+ cameras at 90 fps was all developed in-house.

We will add these details to the final version of the paper.

> **Q5.** [...] did the authors also experiment with video compression [...]?

**A5:** We have experimented with video compression before, but have consistently decided against it because it considerably increases the complexity of decoding, in particular, by making random access difficult and more computationally expensive. We believe it might be worth revisiting this in a couple of years, once hardware video decoders (such as AV1 of the Macbook M3 and the H.265 decoder of the Raspberry Pi 5) become commonplace.

> **Q6.** Could the authors clarify if the methods discussed in Section 3 released together with the data were actually trained on Ava-256 and/or Goliath-4?

The methods in S3 span a number of years, and some of them were trained on slightly different datasets at the time of publication; however, 
* They have been re-trained on Ava-256 and Goliath-4 for this release
* They have been re-worked for OSS release; for example, they all share CUDA utilities, evaluation code, and dataloading, facilitating comparisons and future work

The methods are not new, but their release as OSS is new and tightly coupled to the two datasets introduced in this paper.

> **D1.** What sort of contingency plans do authors have for [withdrawal of consent]?

**AD1:** For Ava-256 we have 77 additional captures that could be used to replace the publicly available ones.
For Goliath-4, we have 124 additional sets of captures available for replacement.

> **D2.** What sort of pathways have subjects to withdraw consent of their data, and how can we make reproducibility / benchmarks based on this dataset transparent on this reality if there are changes to the composition of the data?

**AD2:** The subjects should get in touch with the maintainers of the dataset (julietamartinez@meta.com, javierromero1@meta.com) to express their desire to withdraw their consent. Complying with those wishes is at odds with keeping the composition of the data constant over time. We have replacement captures, will version the release, and re-run and re-publish baselines in case of changes to the data.

**References:**
[1] Ha, H. et al, "Deltille grids for geometric camera calibration" CVPR 17

title.value: Dataset for the Complete, Driveable, and Generalizable Avatars

summary_and_contributions.value:
To improve the generalization and driveability, this work proposes a dataset of 256 subjects captured in two modalities and a dataset
of 4 subjects captured in eight modalities towards completeness. Based on the data, this work further provides code and pre-trained models for different state-ofthe-art human generation models. The key contributions are the quality, paired labels, and pre-trained models to benefit the area.

review.value:
Quality: good. This work is easy to read, and the overall contributions of the proposed datasets have high quality.
Clarity: good. This work has a clear target to improve the generalization, driveability, and completeness. Some results are also promising.
Originality: borderline. The overall data capture device is the key to the quality of the dataset. However, the diversity of the captured data is still limited. Many previous works have proposed captured datasets.
Significance: somewhat good. The quality and paired modalities are beneficial to the community. However, I am still concerned about the diversity and quantity of the dataset to boost the generalization and performance on specific tasks and models.

strengths.value:
1. The main contributions of this work are the quality, paired modalities, and models, which will boost this area towards complete, driveable, and generalizable avatars. The captured device is quite important to this work, and it is valuable.
2. The overall writing and presentation are good.
3. Comprehensive data information, statistics, usage, comparisons are introduced.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. The usage and models for this data should be further discussed in the main paper, including comparisons of trained models on previous datasets and the effectiveness of the data on the provided tasks. 
2. The validation of the data, paired modalities should be improved. Show more qualitative and quantitative results.
3. In the related work, add one more table to compare with existing body avatars and hand avatars.

limitations.value:
1. The main issue of this work is about the quantity. Although the size is large (32TB), the IDs, sentences and expressions are limited compared with previous head and body avatar datasets, making the in-the-wild generalization poor. 
2. The effectiveness validation of this dataset is limited. More qualitative and quantitative results would be convincing.

correctness.value: This work introduces a dataset, and it is constructed in a sound way.

clarity.value: Yes, this work is easy to read.

relation_to_prior_work.value: Yes, in the related work, this work discussed the head, hand, and body avatar generation datasets. Comprehensive comparisons in a table could be better.

ethics.value: The potential ethics has been discussed in the main paper (human subjects).

title.value: An extensive dataset for codec avatar

summary_and_contributions.value: This work provides a dataset of 256 subjects captured in a high-resolution dome and another dataset of 4 subjects under 8 modalities.

review.value: This is an excellent work that can promote the evolution of digital human related fields. However, it looks more like a technical report.

strengths.value:
1 This work has a large economic cost and a large data set. The open-source avatar data will contribute to the community.
2 This work considers different parts of the avatar. In addition to the common head, the body, hands, and other areas are carefully modeled. These advantages are more intuitively reflected in the visualization in the paper.
3 The maintenance of the relevant code is perfect and executable.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1 The compression protocol used can be improved. Compared with 2D, 3D data such as Avatar is very large, so a higher compression rate is required. The compression rate of JPEG and other methods used in this work is limited. It is recommended to use more advanced VVC, WEBP, etc.
2 The main contribution of this article lies in the dataset, but what advantages does this dataset have compared to previous ones? For example, is the semantic segmentation provided in Assets more accurate than the previous ones? Or is using this large-scale dataset to train tasks such as avatar singing better than a small-scale one? These all require objective indicators, and the indicators listed in Table 2 alone are not enough to prove the advantages. In other words, articles in the db track need to explain and solve a certain problem or address a problem that no one before has solved it. If the data scale is just dozens of times larger than the previous work, this article can be an excellent technical report, but not a research paper.

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper proposes a new dataset for drivable and generalisable avatars. Specifically, it offers a collection of captured head data from 256 subjects in two modalities - multiview capture + headset capture. Further, the authors extend the dataset with full body capture for 4 subjects. This includes multiview captures of head, hands, and full body in regular and minimal clothing, followed by corresponding phone captures. Finally, the work provides pretrained models for avatar generation.

review.value:
The paper touches upon a topic that attracts a lot of attention in the research community, namely photorealistic drivable avatar generation. The authors mention that it is crucial to have low and high-resolution data per subject in order to develop generalisable methods for avatar creation. To this end, the work proposes a new dataset of multimodal capture. Namely, it introduces a dataset of paired captures of human heads for 256 subjects. This includes images from high-resolution multi-view capture setup as well as headset internal camera capture. The inclusion of low-resolution modality is the most differentiating factor with respect to other large-scale datasets (as shown in Table 2). Given the current higher popularity of phones as a capture device as compared to VR/AR headsets, it is a bit of a missed opportunity not to include such a capture as a part of the dataset, especially as the authors had the capture protocol ready, use the phone capture for full body. It would give the work a much broader scope. 

The second part of the dataset release is 4 subjects captured in a full-body manner. A high-quality capture of a dynamic body has been explored in the literature (e.g. [1]). An additional value is provided through the inclusion of various modalities in the capture, i.e. including head and hand, full and minimal clothing captures, as well as phone-collected data. Further, Goliath-4 provides head and hand captures under varying illumination. With respect to data in Goliath-4, it would be good if the authors described the procedure of obtaining segmentation masks, keypoints, 3d reconstructions. I believe that such a high-quality data release is very beneficial for researchers, I am slightly in doubt whether it goes along the claim of generalisability, especially as it was not proven through experiments.

The authors of this work pay particular attention to investigating the trade-off between the compression level, and quality of data. It is a very good effort towards releasing high-quality data within a storage budget. Aside from the dataset, the paper provides various state-of-the-art models and their extensions trained on the released data. Firstly, a multi-person face model is provided to disentangle identity and expressions, followed by an extension enabling the use of expression latent code obtained from the headset capture. Similarly, models for relightable head and hand avatars are provided. Finally, a full-body avatar model is suggested. This is a nice amount of models provided along the dataset, facilitating its use by other researchers. What I am missing in this regard, are numerical comparisons. It is mainly up to authors to select works that use similar data (e.g. these can be works used as baseline models here) and provide comparisons that would emphasise the benefits of the use of the proposed dataset. 

In summary, the authors proposed a large, well-designed dataset, that will be useful to the research community. However, it could be better motivated and provided with experimental results.

strengths.value:
- The dataset contains a large amount of captured data. The capture setups as such are not a commonly available tool in the research community. Therefore, high-quality data release is always welcomed.
- The authors of this paper pay particular attention to investigating the trade-off between storage size, decompression speed, and the quality of the data included in a release of the dataset. I believe that a reasonable dataset release size is important in conducting research on avatar generation, especially in an academic setting.
- There are several pretrained models provided with the data. This is great for providing a starting point for researchers to use.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- I believe that the head capture could have been done including the data captured using a phone which was done for the body. This is due to a couple of reasons. Mainly, as of today phones are significantly more popular devices than headsets in non-research settings. This would significantly strengthen the argument of pairing the high-quality, very exclusive capture with a common device. Additionally, headset capture is very particular in its specification - field of view, monochromatism. This makes the dataset less general, targeted mainly at headset-related research.
- Full body data include segmentation masks, keypoints, 3d reconstructions. It would be great to describe how those were obtained (and to what precision if possible).
- Was the head capture with changing lighting conditions done only for the 4 subjects? It is mentioned that the same system is used for the head in Goliath as it is in Ava.
- There are no experimental results included. This is typically used to prove the soundness of a new dataset and motivate the necessity for the dataset in the community. In this case, the authors already trained some models on their data, hence, comparing it with other datasets (where applicable) is a natural follow-up. Where a new modality is introduced (e.g. headset capture) such an experiment is not feasible and only qualitative samples are sufficient.
- It would be great to see some qualitative results for the generalisable face encoder - it is the experiment that greatly corresponds to the generalisability claim.

limitations.value: The authors provide a brief limitation section in which they correctly identified some main limitations of their released data. They noticed limited generalizability on relightable head avatars. Similarly, they point out that the 4-subject Goliath dataset has a limited research scope.

correctness.value: The dataset is constructed soundly. The data collected is of high quality and has been curated well for public release.

clarity.value: The paper is well-written, and I had no trouble following it.

relation_to_prior_work.value:
Due to the relatively high number of other multi-view face datasets, the authors put a detailed section containing factors differentiating the dataset from prior works.

I believe that ActorsHQ [1] should be cited and briefly compared to. Similarly, DNA-Rendering [2] could be looked at as a comparison.

documentation.value:
The release and maintenance are described clearly.

The datasheet of the dataset is provided and contains a lot of details.

There are some elements of the capture procedure that could be included:
- the procedure of obtaining non-captured modalities
- what is the capture scenario - the prompt used by RA could be documented

ethics.value: The data that is released in this work contain human subjects. The methodology of capture is described in the paper. The subjects were compensated for the work and signed consent for capture and release (Sec. 2). Regarding question 11 in *Collection Process* within the dataset's datasheet, it is mentioned that subjects may drop out at any time during the study (capture). What is the mechanism of revoking the consent post-capture and post-release?

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 1: Yes, there are significant ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
Questions:
- Table 2, and Table 1 in the Appendix show a large difference in dataset size between Ava and RenderMe. Where does the difference come from? Is it the length of the captures? It does not feel like the inclusion of headset capture would result in a 5-fold size increase.

References:

[2] Wei Cheng, Ruixiang Chen, Wanqi Yin, Siming Fan, Keyu Chen, Honglin He, Huiwen Luo, Zhongang Cai, Jingbo Wang, Yang Gao, Zhengming Yu, Zhengyu Lin, Daxuan Ren, Lei Yang, Ziwei Liu, Chen Change Loy, Chen Qian, Wayne Wu, Dahua Lin, Bo Dai, Kwan-Yee Lin. title.value: Interesting capture set-up for human reconstruction, with limited scale

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper introduces two datasets concerned with 3d human reconstruction captured with state-of-the-art capture systems (e.g. camera domes or lightstages) paired with more casual set-ups (e.g. smartphone, headset cameras), namely Ava-256, and Goliath-4. Ava-256 contains 256 subjects, captured in a face lightstage, which is paired with a repeated capture where the subjects wears a commercial headset  equipped with infrared cameras to be used for expression transfer. Goliath-4 includes 4 subjects captured in a full-body lightstage (clothed and with minimal clothing), together with head and hand captures from the ava-256 dome set-up and smartphone captures. The authors also provide several other assets extracted from the raw data, e.g. 3d mesh tracking, semantic segmentation, 3d keypoints. This submission also mentions code release of a number of reconstruction models for head, hand and full body, even though to the best of my knowledge those are effectively works reviewed and published previously with no additional contributions to be evaluated within this submission.

review.value:
I believe this dataset to be of sufficient quality and of interest for publication to the wider community.

In summary, the dataset contains data captured with state-of-the-art capture systems, of very high quality and definition, which is rarely accessible to a number of research labs (see strengths for a complete list). On the cons side, I believe the scale of this dataset to be lacking compared to recent dataset releases, e.g. MVHumanNet [A] or DNA-Render [B], and find some of the claims and story line in the paper to overrepresent the scale of the dataset (e.g. use for generalization and completeness of avatar reconstruction). Arguably the most distinctive feature of the data is the paired headset and smartphone captures, even though this is not discussed or motivated into a lot of depth in the manuscript, and is also unclear why each dataset have different pairings. Finally, authors should address missing information with regards to consent management and dataset integrity (see Documentation box), and aim at providing as much technical details as they possibly can with respect to the actual capturing system. 

In order to keep the accept rating, I would like the authors to address at least these concerns satisfactorily.

strengths.value:
+ The paper is well written and generally clear about the scope and contents of the datasets
+ Both the 2.4m and 5.5m high-resolution domes are state-of-the-art capture set-ups producing very high definition data which is otherwise difficult to get access to by a majority of research labs
+ Coupling the high-end expensive captures with smartphone captures is an ideal case to foster casual capture of human bodies via readily available sensors 
+ Incorporating headset mounted cameras could be interesting as it might bring attention to the difficulty of driving human avatars while wearing a closed headset due to the imaging pipeline differences, and the naturally oblique camera angles
+ The authors prepare differently sizes versions of the dataset to foster accessibility to researchers who might have limited internet access and/or storage capabilities.  
+ There is already a website in place (accessible via links in the suppl. material) with additional information on the dataset composition and links to the data download.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. I find the claims on the use of the datasets towards generalizable reconstruction and "complete" models to be an overrepresentation of the dataset (note this is in the title of the submission), specially given that the scale on the "complete" data is very limited at only 4 subject identities. Refer to correctness box for more details on this.
2. Recent dataset releases, such as MVHumanNet (full body, +5000 subjects), DNA-Rendering, RenderMe have order of magnitudes more identities while also keeping a dense sampling of cameras at high resolution. In essence, this means Ava-256 and Goliath-4 might be outdate quickly in terms of scale. Refer to Relation to prior art box for more details on this.
3. I found the discussion around the use and design of the headset infrared cameras to be fairly shallow, and this is arguably the most important differentiating factor with respect to other current face datasets (as depicted in Table 2). Why is it important that we can drive avatars while wearing a big VR closed headset? This seems to be a design choice based on the choice of visualization. People transmitting an avatar but possibly visualizing on e.g. 3D holographic display or open glasses might face substantially different challenges.
4. In general the submission is not providing a lot of technical details and insight about the exact composition of the capturing set-up (e.g. camera and light models, calibration procedures). If the authors are able to, I believe the submission would be greatly improved by incorporating this information together with the insights and the sort of design choices and challenges the authors faced while building the system.
5. With respect to compression, did the authors also experiment with video compression, e.g. H265 or VP9 if preferring open source ? As some of this data is indeed a sequence of frames it seems an obvious choice for additional compression gains.
6. Could the authors clarify if the methods discussed in Section 3 released together with the data were actually trained on Ava-256 and/or Goliath-4? If not, I do not see why exactly would they be part of the dataset release, as the methods were published in prior venues and might not have any tight connection to the data discussed in this submission.

limitations.value: Authors discuss limitations and negative societal impact in the submission. Arguably, authors could revise and extend this with further information about the management of consent of the captured subjects, and discuss into more details their limitations when it comes to scale when compared with existing literature, e.g. MVHumanNet.

correctness.value:
The proposed pipeline seems to be well designed, and the captures seems to have been performed to a high standard.

With respect to the claims correctness, I do find the claims on the use of the datasets towards generalizable reconstruction and "complete" models to be an overrepresentation of the dataset (note this is in the title of the submission), specially given that the scale on the "complete" data is very limited at only 4 subject identities. Authors do discuss some of these limitations on the limitations section, however I find the introduction section to be overly relying on these two themes (with the numbered conditions that models should fulfil). I find it difficult to argue that this dataset aims at complete and generalizable human reconstruction (with only 4 ids with complete body, and a relatively modest id count on the head capture of 256 identities), and would much rather prefer that the authors discuss and introduce this dataset on its own merits as a high quality head dataset, with the novelty of introducing headset-mounted camera views and possibly soften their claims on full-body completeness and generalization unless they are willing or able to match the scale of the Goliath-4 dataset accordingly.

clarity.value: The manuscript is generally well-written. If authors were to further improve the clarity of the manuscript, I would suggest to outline in a schematic way the contents of each dataset as early as possible. As it stands, both Ava-256 and Goliath-4 have slightly different data set-ups (e.g. captured with uniform vs directive group lightning, smartphone capture vs headset capture), but this is not outlined in any figure or table in a unified way (i.e. reader needs to finalize page 5 to exactly know what is inside of Goliath-4 dataset). An overview figure or table (similar to e.g. Table 2 but focused on the proposed two datasets) early on would be helpful to give the reader a quick overview of what's in each dataset before going into more depth.

relation_to_prior_work.value:
Authors discuss similar recent head datasets, but miss other relevant prior art related with full body human datasets. Recent dataset releases, such as MVHumanNet [A] (full body, 5000 subjects), DNA-Rendering [B] (full body, >1500 subjects), RenderMe (head, 500 subjects) have order of magnitudes more identities while also keeping a dense sampling of cameras at high resolution. In essence, this means Ava-256 and Goliath-4 might be outdated quickly in terms of scale. Would authors consider releasing more identities to make the dataset more competitive to [A, B]? Could authors discuss in which ways Ava-256 or Goliath-4 are improving over prior art?

**References**  
[A] Z Xiong et al., "MVHumanNet: A Large-scale Dataset of Multi-view Daily  
Dressing Human Captures. In CVPR 2024  
[B] W Chen et al., "DNA-Rendering: A Diverse Neural Actor Repository for High-Fidelity Human-centric Rendering". In ICCV 2023

documentation.value:
Authors discuss briefly the maintenance in the supplementary material (i.e. via s3 bucket in AWS), however there is very little information about how the authors might handle withdrawals of consents by the captured subjects, which is specially problematic for Goliath-4 where a few subjects withdrawing consent might compromise the integrity of the dataset. 

D1. What sort of contingency plans do authors have for this? 
D2. What sort of pathways have subjects to withdraw consent of their data, and how can we make reproducibility / benchmarks based on this dataset transparent on this reality if there are changes to the composition of the data?

ethics.value: Authors do address some important aspects of their work in terms of ethical implications (e.g. human subject treatment and remuneration, distribution of seIf-reported skin-tone), nonetheless I believe these datasets warrant additional ethics discussion and review as it does involve several categories for ethics flags, namely human subject research, fairness, data privacy and consent - the later with little to no discussion at all in the manuscript.

title.value: Codec Avatar Studio: Paired Human Captures for Complete, Driveable, and Generalizable Avatars

abstract.value:
To build photorealistic avatars that users can embody, human modelling must be complete (cover the full body), driveable (able to reproduce the current motion and appearance from the user), and generalizable (_i.e._, easily adaptable to novel identities).
Towards these goals, _paired_ captures, that is, captures of the same subject obtained from systems of diverse quality and availability, are crucial.
However, paired captures are rarely available to researchers outside of dedicated industrial labs: _Codec Avatar Studio_ is our proposal to close this gap.
Towards generalization and driveability, we introduce a dataset of 256 subjects captured in two modalities: high resolution multi-view scans of their heads, and video from the internal cameras of a headset.
Towards completeness, we introduce a dataset of 4 subjects captured in eight modalities: high quality relightable multi-view captures of heads and hands, full body multi-view captures with minimal and regular clothes, and corresponding head, hands and body phone captures.
Together with our data, we also provide code and pre-trained models for different state-of-the-art human generation models.
Our datasets and code are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/ava-256 and https://github.com/facebookresearch/goliath.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
